extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners before the USPTO (respondents in OED reciprocal discipline proceedings), OED staff, USPTO counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 (Selling v. Radford framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO reciprocal-discipline rule (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)) / Selling standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) the imposition of the same sanction by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline is presumptively proper under Selling v. Radford; the regulation mirrors Selling. The USPTO will impose the identical sanction unless the respondent meets the stated burdens for one of the four listed exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for preventing reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that there is a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the Selling/§11.24(d)(1) elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO treat this standard as narrow and difficult to satisfy; the Director is not sitting as an appellate court to retry the state proceeding. See In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich, and related authority cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process inquiry (Selling element (i) / §11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires meaningful notice and an opportunity to be heard — e.g., notice of charges, attendance and active participation, ability to present evidence and witnesses, testify, cross-examine, and make argument. Mere disagreement with rulings (e.g., denial of a continuance) or procedural rulings is not necessarily a due process deprivation. Cases and USPTO precedent set out that being present, participating, and having evidentiary opportunities satisfies due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof inquiry (Selling element (ii) / §11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult showing. Deference is given to the state factfinder; credibility determinations generally receive deference. Mere disagreement with findings, claims of evidentiary errors, or complaints about weight of evidence do not ordinarily establish infirmity of proof. Respondent must show an infirmity so substantial that accepting the state sanction would be inconsistent with the USPTO's duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice inquiry (Selling element (iii) / §11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether imposition of the same sanction by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct. Consider whether the state sanction was within the appropriate range of penalties and relevant mitigating factors. If state discipline falls within the appropriate range, reciprocal discipline ordinarily is not a 'grave injustice.' Re-arguing the underlying findings does not satisfy this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that the practitioner was not publicly disciplined (Selling element (iv) / §11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must raise and support any contention that the predicate state action did not amount to one of the listed public disciplinary actions; failure to address the actual predicate judgment (e.g., the Massachusetts Amended Judgment) is failure to meet burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal proceedings are not de novo reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's reciprocal-discipline proceeding is not a de novo retrial of the state disciplinary proceedings; the inquiry is limited to the Selling/§11.24(d)(1) exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director will not act as an appellate body to discover error in the state hearing judge's or courts' proceedings; garden-variety errors, conflicting interpretations, or credibility disputes ordinarily do not prevent reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's procedural obligations in USPTO Notice and Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must file a response to the Director's Notice and Order containing all information the respondent believes sufficient to establish, by clear and convincing evidence, a genuine issue of material fact that imposition of identical discipline would be unwarranted; the Notice provided 40 days to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent should specifically address the state judgment the USPTO predicates its reciprocal discipline upon. Bypassing the predicate state judgment or failing to present clear-and-convincing evidence as to a Selling element will cause the respondent to fail its burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of misconduct supporting state disbarment (behaviors leading to discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: State court findings cited for revocation/disbarment included: providing incorrect legal advice; continuing to represent clients after representation terminated; refusing to return unearned fees; refusing to release former client documents to new counsel; providing false documents; failing to provide documentation; lying to an investigator; failing to timely file pleadings; failing to schedule hearings; not communicating with clients reasonably; making false statements to clients to earn more money; charging excessive fees; failing to deposit advance fees into trust; allowing staff to make false statements; submitting fraudulent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples illustrate the kinds of attorney misconduct that may support state disbarment and thus predicate reciprocal discipline under USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition to conclude pending matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is granted limited recognition for thirty (30) days to conclude work on behalf of clients on any matters pending before the Office; if work cannot be concluded within 30 days, respondent must advise each client so they may make other arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited recognition is strictly time-limited and intended only to allow wrapping up existing matters; after the limited-recognition period expires, additional prohibitions and account restrictions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO account and access prohibitions post-exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective upon expiration of the 30-day limited recognition, USPTO may disable/suspend any USPTO.gov accounts registered to respondent; respondent shall not apply for or obtain a USPTO verified Electronic System account, have his name added to another's account, verify others' credentials, or sponsor USPTO.gov accounts for filing until reinstated pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO is authorized to prevent access and to enforce account restrictions; respondent remains responsible for any re-activation efforts and may not attempt to circumvent prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirements for final orders
rubrics_metrics.description: OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the order's notice language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final disciplinary actions are publicly disclosed in OED's FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette as part of transparency and notice to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to judicial review / filing timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of the USPTO Director's final decision may be had by a petition filed with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents seeking to challenge the Director's final order must file timely in the Eastern District of Virginia per statute and local rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5).
